INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
The International Municipal Lawyers
Association (“IMLA”) is the nation’s oldest and largest
organization devoted solely to promoting local
government law.  A nonprofit, nonpartisan,
professional association, IMLA’s membership
comprises more than 2,500 local government entities,
including cities, counties, and subdivisions thereof, as
represented by their chief legal officers, state
municipal leagues, and individual attorneys.  IMLA’s
mission is to advance the responsible development of
municipal law through education and advocacy by
providing the collective viewpoint of local
governments around the country on legal issues
before the Supreme Court of the United States, the
United States Courts of Appeals, and state supreme
and appellate courts.
The National Association of Counties (“NACo”)
is the only national organization that represents
county governments in the United States.  Founded in
1935, NACo provides essential services to the nation’s
3,069 counties through advocacy, education, and
research.
Amici offer their perspective on why Alaska’s
forfeiture law is entitled to substantial deference .
Amici also provide valuable context, from a local
government perspective, that underscores why
Petitioner’s proposed Eighth Amendment paradigm
would intrude on legislative prerogatives, undermine

basic principles of federalism  and the successful
exercise of local government, and infringe on
indigenous Alaskan communities’ sovereignty
interests.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Petitioner has asked this Court to clarify the
inquiry that courts must undertake when assessing
whether a fine or forfeiture contravenes the Eighth
Amendment’s Excessive Fines Clause.  Petitioner
asserts that courts assessing the gravity of harm
caused by  a criminal violation are limited to a
defendant’s individualized wrongdoing, and  cannot
consider the broader societal damage caused by a
particular crime.  That pinhole perspective will invite
a torrent of Eighth Amendment litigation.
Petitioner’s invitation also sets the wrong course.  The
setting of criminal penalties has always called for a
broader outlook.  Criminal punishment is equally
rooted in the social contract and the broader social
good.
This Court’s analysis must begin with the
fundamental premise of United States v. Bajakajian ,
524 U.S. 321 (1998)—that legislatures, not courts, are
delegated the power to define criminal punishments.
Those definitions reflect policy choices, compromises,
and the political accountability of the legislative
branch.  Bajakajian calls for deference to those
legislative judgments.
Alaska’s mandatory aircraft forfeiture does not
run afoul of the Constitution.  As an in personam
penalty, this forfeiture cannot be seen as a State’s
avarice.  There is no money grab as in rem forfeiture
might be characterized .  I nstead, mandatory

3

forfeiture serves as a productive and reasonable
deterrent.  It was reasonably designed to give teeth to
the State’s Local Option system.
It also reflects a success of local democracy.
The Local Option system  empowers the communities
most grievously impacted by alcohol abuse to use the
democratic process to limit or prohibit access to
alcohol.  Th ose communities have overwhelmingly
chosen to keep or strengthen restrictions, supported
by the enforcement mechanism at issue.  And these
restrictions have achieved documented successes in
reducing crime and adverse public health outcomes.
Mandatory forfeiture evolved through an
iterative, legislative process, and only after the
Legislature determined a discretionary scheme was
ineffective.  This particular legislative scheme  might
not make sense everywhere.  But it does make sense
in Alaska, where aircraft offer the primary, and often
the only, means for smuggling and bootlegging into
remote, rural communities .  As a result,  the risk of
forfeiture is a keystone for criminal deterrence.
The stakes for enforcement are incredibly high.
Dry communities do not have the public health or law
enforcement resources, let alone the necessary funds,
to address the scourge of alcohol abuse .  E ffectively
stemming the flow of alcohol into these remote
communities is central to protecting their health,
safety, and economic vitality.
Undermining Alaska’s Local Option system,
and the forfeiture law that enforces it, would not only
override the Legislature’s considered judgment.  It
would undermine the autonomy and self -
determination of indigenous communities that the

4

law was designed to serve.  The judgment of the
Alaska Supreme Court should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. Legislative Determinations In Crafting
Criminal Penalties Are Entitled To
Substantial Deference
A. Bajakajian’s Excessiveness
Standard Is Deferential To
Legislative Judgments
As this Court held in  Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at
334, forfeitures may not be “grossly disproportional”
to the gravity o f an offense.  To derive an
excessiveness standard, this Court articulated two
relevant controlling principles: (1) “judgments about
the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in
the first instance to the legislature,” and (2) “any
judicial determination” regarding the gravity of a
criminal offense is “inherently imprecise.”  Id. at 336.
Under this scheme, a forfeiture only needs to “bear
some relationship to the gravity of the offense.”  Id. at
334 (emphasis added).  Courts owe “substantial
deference” to legislatures’ “broad authority ” to
determine the “types and limits of punishments for
crimes.”  Id. at 336 (quoting Solem v. Helm, 463 U.S.
277, 290 (1983)).
Bajakajian’s deference is consistent with the
longstanding rule that legislatures—not courts —are
delegated the power to define criminal punishments.
Chapman v. United States , 500 U.S. 453, 467 (1991).
Setting criminal penalties involves “difficult policy
choices.”  Ewing v. California, 538 U.S. 11, 28 (2003);
Rummel v. Estelle , 445 U.S. 263, 28 3 (1980)

5

(“Penologists themselves have been unable to agree
whether sentences should be light or heavy,
discretionary or determinate.”).
Federal courts “do not sit as a ‘superlegislature’
to second-guess” legislatures.  Ewing, 538 U.S. at 28.
A legislature need only have a “reasonable basis” to
believe that its sentencing scheme “advances the goals
of its criminal justice system in any substantial way.”
Id.
Deference further reflects the political
accountability of the legislative branch.  Legislatures
“make policy and bring to bear the collective wisdom
of the whole people when they do, while courts
dispense the judgment of only a single person or a
handful.”  Democratic Nat’l Comm. v. Wis. State
Legislature, 592 U.S. 1039, 1041 (2020) (Gorsuch, J.,
concurring in denial of application to vacate stay).  In
that role, legislatures deploy “far greater resources for
research and factfinding” than “can be mustered in
litigation between discrete parties before a si ngle
judge.”  Id.  Legislation is a product of  “compromise”
and reflects “the broad social consensus necessary to
enact new laws, something not easily replicated in
courtrooms where typically one side must win and the
other lose.”  Id. at 1041-42.
It also reflects institutional expertise.  Federal
judges cannot “begin to ‘match’ the collective wisdom
the American people possess in deciding ‘how best to
handle’” pressing and intractable social problems.
City of Grants Pass v. Johnson , 603 U.S. 520, 560
(2024).  Legislatures may “experiment with one set of
approaches only to find later another set works better”
or “they may find certain responses more appropriate
for some communities than others.”  Id.  States

6

continue to act as laboratories of democracy by
adopting local solutions to local problems; in some
cases, criminalizing what other state s allow.  As this
Court recognized in Grants Pass , the Eighth
Amendment serves “many important functions,” but
it “does not authorize federal judges to wrest those
rights and responsibilities” away from the legislative
sphere, which is most accountable to the democratic
process.  Id.
Substantial deference to legislatures’ broad
authority to define criminal punishments  restrains
courts “from an extended analysis of proportionality
save in rare cases.”  United States v. MacEwan , 445
F.3d 237, 247 -48 (3d Cir. 2006) .  This is further
consistent with the rule that courts do  not even
require a “legislature to articulate its reasons for
enacting a statute.”  F.C.C. v. Beach Comm c’ns, Inc.,
508 U.S. 307, 315 (1993) (“a legislative choice is not
subject to courtroom fact -finding”).  Thus, if the
government provides a “commonsense explanation or
some—even relatively weak —evidence” to justify a
fine or forfeiture, “it will likely prevail against an
Excessive Fines Clause challenge. ”  Diamond Sands
Apartments, LLC v. Clark County Nevada , 164 F.4th
759, 764 (9th Cir. 2026).
B. Courts Properly Consider Harm To
The Government In Assessing
Proportionality
Among the Bajakajian factors to assess
proportionality is “the nature and extent of the harm
suffered by the government.”  Pimentel v. City of Los
Angeles, 115 F.4th 1062, 1067 (9th Cir. 2024).

7

This is not an abstract inquiry, but neither is it
limited to one specific defendant’s wrongdoing.  The
social contract —and principles of deterrence —have
always required a broader assessment.  See, e.g.,
Bennis v. Michigan , 516 U.S. 442, 4 53 (1996)
(upholding forfeiture of jointly owned car, deferring to
State law designed “to deter illegal activity that
contributes to neighborhood deterioration and unsafe
streets”).
In assessing proportionality, Courts of Appeals
consistently look at the bigger picture.  For example,
in U.S. Securities & Exchange Commission v. Murphy,
50 F.4th 832, 850 (9th Cir. 2022) , the Ninth Circuit
upheld approximately $2.5 million in penalties for a
bond-flipping scheme , even though the appellants’
violations did not harm any investors .  The penalties
were proportional because the  appellants’ failure to
comply with registration requirements undermined
an “important system of government oversight.”  Id.
Similarly, in United States v. Castello, 611 F.3d
116, 118, 123 -24 (2d Cir.  2010), the Second Circuit
affirmed a $12,012,924 forfeiture for failure to file
currency transaction reports , even though the
defendant had been acquitted of tax fraud and related
crimes.  The court underscored  that defendant’s
failure to file reports “allowed others to commit
crimes” that  the government  otherwise “could have
prevented or prosecuted.”  Id. at 124.
Vasudeva v. United States , 214 F.3d 1155,
1160-61 (9th Cir. 2000) upheld fines of up to $40,000,
even where the defendant store owners did not benefit
from a fraudulent food stamp scheme.  The Ninth
Circuit weighed the broader social ills caused by
defendants’ misconduct.  B ecause “trafficking in food

8

stamps is a serious offense that defrauds the federal
government and undermines the viability of an
important government program for the needy ,” the
penalty was appropriate.  Id.
In upholding the forfeiture of Kenneth Jouppi’s
plane, the Alaska Supreme Court followed the same
playbook.  The court deferred to “the legislature’s
judgment on the gravity of his offense” and it
considered the harm of illegal alcohol smuggling to
the government writ large.  Jouppi v. Alaska, 566 P.3d
943, 956-57 (Alaska 2025); see also Alaska v. Jouppi,
519 P.3d 653, 670 , 675  (Alaska Ct. App. 2022)
(Mannheimer, J., concurring in part and dissenting in
part) (deferring to “reasoned legislative response to a
serious social problem” that empowers rural
communities to prohibit the sale or possession of
alcohol coupled with mandatory forfeiture to “punish
and deter” violators).
The Alaska Supreme Court ’s decision  also
respected the local community’s democratic choice to
restrict access to alcohol under the state’s Local
Option system.  Beaver, Alaska sits a long way from
Washington, D .C.  Its isolation and distance should
not obscure its right to choose; its decision to remain
dry should be respected, deferred to and not
undermined.
C. Mandatory Forfeiture Is A Familiar
Tool Of Criminal Deterrence
The Alaska legislature’s mandatory forfeiture
law is unique to the particular needs of its remote,
rural communities.  But legislatures’ need to employ
mandatory criminal penalties, including forfeiture, as

9

an effective tool for criminal deterrence is neither
special, nor controversial.
Mandatory sentences are legion throughout the
federal criminal justice system and in the States.  For
instance, the United States Sentencing Commission
has identified 195 federal statutes that carry
mandatory minimum penalties. 2  In fiscal year 2025,
13,926 of the 66,662 federal cases reported to the
Commission—20 percent—involved an offense
carrying a mandatory minimum penalty. 3  Each of
these statutes fixes punishment by the category of
conduct, not by the individual defendant’s
circumstances.
State and local governments similarly resort to
mandatory criminal forfeiture when warranted.
Take, for example, the evolving problems of “street
takeovers.”  Galvanized by social media, street
takeovers occur when huge crowds surround city
intersections to watch people engaging in dangerous
horseplay with vehicles spin around at ever increasing
speeds.  The result can be as tragic as it is predictable.
Participants can be injured or killed, but there have
also been multiple fatalities among spectators and
innocent bystanders.4

2 U.S. Sent’g Comm’n, Report to the  Congress: Mandatory
Minimum Penalties in the Federal Criminal Justice System, 348
n. 838 (2011).
3  U.S. Sent’g Comm’n, Quick Facts: Mandatory Minimum

10

State legislatures should be empowered to
include mandatory forfeiture in connection with this
kind of criminal conduct if other deterrents continue
to fail.5  Local governments, exercising the forfeiture
authority that state law confers, are already
experimenting with forfeitures related to illegal street
takeovers, and in some cases, destroying the vehicles
to deter crime. 6  A ruling in favor of Petitioner risks
undermining state and local governments’ abilities to
effectively deter a myriad of public safety threats.
D. Alaska’s Forfeiture Laws Reflect A
Carefully Crafted Response To A
Public Health And Safety Crisis
Alaska’s forfeiture statute was not enacted in a
vacuum.  It was the product of a decades -long
legislative process in response to a public health and
safety crisis, informed by extensive testimony, peer -
reviewed research, and the lived experience of
Alaska’s Native communities.

Nathan Solis & Melissa Hernandez, Inside L.A.'s Deadly Street
Takeover Scene: 'A Scene of Lawlessness' , L.A. Times (Aug. 22,
2022), .
5 Law enforcement often lacks the resources to stop street
takeovers while they are in progress.  Large crowds may become
hostile, and there have been instances of officers being attacked
and patrol cars being crashed into, which makes combatting the
problem more challenging.  See id.

1. The Legislature’s Iterative,
Evidence-Based Response
Alcoholism and alcohol -related crime in
Alaska’s rural communities  has been a documented
public health and safety emergency without parallel
in the lower 48 States .  Alcohol abuse  presents
massive problems that have persistently plagued
these communities, which often lack adequate police
and health-care resources to respond.
The Legislature first took action in response to
several, comprehensive studies that documented the
extent of alcohol-related abuse, the economic costs of
that abuse, and the close association between alcohol
and crime, particularly in rural communities.
Harrison v. Alaska, 687 P.2d 332, 335, 339 (Alaska Ct.
App. 1984) (upholding constitutionality of local option
statutory scheme, affirming the “law bears a close and
substantial relationship to the legitimate legislative
goal of protecting the public health and welfare by
curbing the level of alcohol abuse in our state”).
One study, by the Governor’s Commission on
the Administration of Justice, specifically
recommended that rural villages be allowed to control
access to alcoholic beverages.  687 P.2d at 335.
Another reported that, in rural areas, 77.9% of violent
crime and 55.6% of property crimes were committed
under the influence of alcohol.  Id.  A third
documented the sheer volume of devastation  caused
by alcoholism , noting Alaska’s alcoholism mortality
rate was 418% higher than the national average ,
consumption was growing at almost twice as fast as
other parts of the country, and was worst  in rural
areas.  Id.  The costs to the State and its people were
staggering.  Abraham v. Alaska, 585 P.2d 526, 532

12

n.19 (Alaska 1978) (noting the total cost of alcohol -
related crime was over 30% of the State’s total
criminal justice expenditures).
Alaska responded to this crisis with the Local
Option system in 1980, giving communities the power
to restrict alcohol through democratic vote. 7  Around
the same time, it developed a forfeiture scheme to give
communities the tools to enforce these laws, deter
violators, and stem the flow of alcohol into
communities.  These laws gave courts the authority to
order the forfeiture of planes, vessels, or vehicles used
to circumvent local option laws.  SLA 1980, ch. 131,
§ 3.
Six years later, the Legislature acted again,
expanding the authority of local communities to
completely ban the possession of alcoholic beverages.
SLA 1986, ch. 80, § 2.  It explained its action in a
series of legislative findings, noting (1) the acute
dangers to public health and safety arising from
alcohol abuse in rural areas, (2) the lack of adequate
health care facilities or law enforcement in these
areas, and (3) the economic reality that these rural
communities could not afford the cost of alcohol abuse.
SLA 1986, ch. 80, § 1, subds. (2), (6), (8).
The Legislature acknowledged that the prior
Local Option statutes had fallen short, by prohibiting
the sale and importation of alcohol, but not personal
possession.  By 1986, the Legislature concluded rural
areas needed the additional authority to impose a

7 Matthew Berman & Teresa Hull, Alcohol Control by
Referendum in Northern Native Communities: The Alaska Local
Option Law, Reports 272 (2000), .

13

total ban to achieve their goals.  SLA 1986, ch. 80, § 1,
subd. (6).
Initially, the Legislature left the forfeiture of
aircraft, vehicles, and boats used to facilitate
smuggling to courts’ discretion.  See Former Alaska
Stat. § 04.16.220(a)(3) (1980).  But it revisited that
issue twenty-four years later, and made the forfeiture
of airplanes mandatory.
This, too, was by design.   At the time the
mandatory forfeiture law was passed, twenty -five
percent of all deaths in Alaska were alcohol -related.8
The Legislature focused on aircraft because of the
primacy of aircraft-facilitated bootlegging and
communities’ otherwise limited means to stop it.
Hearing on S.B. 170 Before the Sen. Judiciary Comm.,
23d Leg., 2d Sess. (Alaska Mar. 10, 2004) at 7
(statement of Susan Parkes, Deputy Att’y Gen.)
(mandatory forfeiture law addresses “problems
primarily found in rural communities” and is “aimed
at strengthening communities’ ability” to enforce their
local option laws).
The penalties had to be stringent to be effective.
Illegal bootlegging in Alaska is a lucrative criminal
enterprise.  The Local Option laws were created with
the express intention of stopping it.  Hearing on S.B.
170 Before the S en. Judiciary Comm., 23d Leg., 2d

8 Bernard Segal, Drinking and Drinking -Related Problems
Among Alaska Natives , 22 Alcohol Health & Res. World 276
(1998).  Those trends have continued.  Alaska’s rate of alcohol -
induced deaths remains the second highest in the nation.  Tony
Wong, et al., Alcohol-induced Deaths in the United States Across
Age, Race, Gender, Geography, and the COVID -19 Pandemic,
PLOS Global Public Health 5(9): e0004623 (Sept. 17, 2025).

14

Sess. (Alaska Mar. 10, 2004) (statement of Lt. Al
Storey) at 21 (“far more money is made per dollar
invested in the alcohol business in Alaska than in the
drug business”).
At the time the law was passed, a $10 bottle of
liquor purchased in Anchorage could be sold for up to
$150 in the far reaches of the State.  Id.  The margins
have only grown more extreme.  In 2025, Alaska State
Troopers estimated that a $10 bottle of liquor could be
sold for “anywhere from $200 -$400 a bottle”
depending on the community. 9  These profit margins
create powerful incentives to exploit the very
transportation infrastructure on which remote
communities depend for survival.
The legislative choice for villages to vote to stay
dry or wet “was requested by rural Alaskans”
themselves, with the express aim that it “would be
enforceable and that its creation would not contribute
to there being a profitable situation for bootleggers .”
Hearing on H.B. 65 Before the H ouse Transp.
Standing Comm., 23d Leg., 1st Sess. (Alaska May 6,
2003) at 11 (statement of Matt Felix, National Council
on Alcohol and Drug Dependence) ; see also id. at 10
(statement of Rep. Bob Lynn)  (“Our Alaska villages
have a right to determine if they are dry or if they are
wet[.]”).10

9 Olivia Nordyke, 150 Bottle of Alcohol Seized in Yukon Delta
Region Bootlegging Arrests, AK News Source (May 30, 2025), .
10 H.B. 65 would have also made forfeiture mandatory for motor
vehicles, aircraft, and vessels. Id. at 10 –11. The House
Transportation Committee heard the bill but  it did not become
law in that form. Id. at 17. During the interim, the Senate
Judiciary Committee added the same bootlegging and forfeiture

15

Mandatory forfeiture of aircraft had  broad
support from the stakeholders that knew the issues
facing rural Alaskan s best.  The Attorney General’s
office touted the due process protections built into the
forfeiture procedure . The State would first have to
prove a violation of the Local Option law beyond a
reasonable doubt, and only then could it seek
forfeiture.  Hearing on H.B. 65 Before the H ouse
Transp. Standing Comm., 23d Leg., 1st Sess. (Alaska
May 6, 2003) at 13 (testimony of Anne Carpeneti,
Assistant Att’y Gen., Criminal Div., Dep’t of Law).
Even the Public Defender Agency recognized the
proposal’s substantial procedural safeguards.  Id. at
11 (testimony of Linda Wilson, Deputy Dir., Public
Defender Agency, Dep’t of Admin.).
In reviewing H.B. 65 and S.B. 170, the
Legislature carefully considered whether mandatory
aircraft forfeiture was necessary to give practical force
to the democratic choices made by dry villages.  A
court that second-guesses that judgment does not just
substitute its own view for the Legislature’s  and the
local community’s ; it overrides a considered policy
informed by decades of evidence that the Local Option
system works—if it can be enforced.

provisions to SB 170. Minutes, Sen. Fin. Comm. (Apr. 16, 2004)
at 13. Those provisions only included mandatory forfeiture of
aircraft.  SB 170, as amended, was enacted as Chapter 124, SLA
2004; Section 11 contains the aircraft forfeiture requirement at
issue here. SLA 2004, ch. 124, § 11.

16

2. The Structure Of The
Forfeiture Statute Reflects
Deliberate Calibration
The Legislature also did not impose a one-sizefits-all forfeiture regime.  For vehicles and watercraft
used to import alcohol into dry communities,
forfeiture is reserved for repeat offenders, felony
probationers, and those transporting at least twice
the quantity presumed for barter or sale.  Alaska Stat.
§ 04.16.220(i)(2); see also id. § 04.11.010(c).
Aircraft are treated more severely because the
Legislature considered aircraft-facilitated bootlegging
a categorically different threat to communities
accessible only by air.  Id. § 04.16.220(i)(1); § I.D.1,
supra.  This graduated structure is the hallmark of a
legislature acting with precision, not arbitrariness.
The Legislature’s calibration extends further.
The forfeiture statute explicitly provides an innocentowner defense, ensuring forfeiture does not reach
property owners who neither knew of nor consented to
the unlawful use. See Alaska Stat. § 04.16.220(e)(2).
The statute evolved over decades of iterative
refinement.  And it is rooted in an even longer State
history of effectively using forfeiture to enforce
smuggling and poaching statutes, and  to deter
violations of those laws.  Jouppi, 519 P.3d at 675 -77
(Mannheimer, J., concurring in part and dissenting in
part) (providing overview of Alaska forfeiture statutes
from 1867 to present day, which included the
forfeiture of airplanes from “the birth of commercial
aviation”); Jordan v. Alaska, 681 P.2d 346, 350
(Alaska Ct. App. 1984) (upholding forfeiture of
defendant’s $10,000 interest in plane following

17

conviction for hunting black bear, as necessary for
deterrence).
This incremental development is itself evidence
of proportionality .  A  legislature that escalates
penalties only after carefully reviewing  whether its
prior legislative efforts have achieved its goals is the
antithesis of acting arbitrarily.
II. “Alaska Is Different” And Those
Differences Matter Here
A. Alaska-Specific Circumstances
Necessitate An Alaska-Specific Law
This Court has regularly recognized that
idiosyncratic conditions necessitate location -specific
law.  See, e.g., Maine v. Taylor, 477 U.S. 131,  150-51
(1986) (upholding Maine’s ban on importing live
baitfish, where importation threatened  fisheries that
were “unique and unusually fragile ”); Hawaii Hous.
Auth. v. Midkiff , 467 U.S. 229,  241-42 (1984)
(upholding land-use condemnation scheme born of a
historic oligopoly originating with early chiefs of the
Hawaiian islands).
This is particularly true for Alaska.  As this
Court has recognized , more than once , “Alaska is
different.”  Sturgeon v. Frost, 577 U.S. 424, 438 (2016).
Its state-specific provisions “reflect the simple truth
that Alaska is often the exception, not the rule.”  Id.
at 440.  “[E]xtreme climate and rugged terrain” make
its residents  uniquely dependent on aircraft,
watercraft, and even hovercraft to reach market, a
hospital, or a home.  Sturgeon v. Frost, 587 U.S. 28, 58
(2019).

18

These differences define how Alaskans live,
how their communities function, and why their
Legislature makes the choices it does.  Over three -
quarters of Alaska’s approximately 300 communities
are located in regions unconnected to the State’s road
system.  Id. at 57.  Alaskans rely on modes of transit
other than roads, “to an extent unknown anyplace else
in the country.”  Id.  For these communities, planes in
the sky are the equivalent of cars on a highway.
The State’s  dry communities exemplify these
dynamics.  (See App. 1a (map of Alaska Local Option
communities).)  They are mostly unconnected by
roads, far from any police station.  (See App. 2a (map
of Alaska law enforcement agencies).)  In these remote
locations, aircraft is the primary means by which
bootleggers smuggle alcohol into dry communities.
And there is minimal law enforcement to stop
it.  Many rural villages are served only by occasional
visits from Alaska State Troopers and, in some cases,
a village public safety officer ( “VPSO”).11  Some
villages do not even have that.  Id.  Even where there
is a police presence, it is sparse at best.  For example,
three officers are tasked with enforcement for 56
villages in the Yukon-Kuskowim Delta area—an area
that spans roughly 58,000 square miles (comparable
in size to the State of New York) and is completely
unconnected to the road system.12

11 Joel Gay, Death Spurs Village to Ban Booze, Anchorage Daily
News (Aug. 15, 2004), .
12 Ben Matheson, A Moving Target: WAANT Pursues Bootleg
Liquor, Alaska Public Media  (Apr. 27, 2015 ), ; About the YK
Delta, Yukon -Kuskokwim Health Corporation , ; Our Region ,
Association of Village Council Presidents, .

19

B. Native Communities’ Democratic
Choice To Remain Dry Should Be
Respected
 The communities most affected by alcohol
abuse in rural Alaska have not been passive observers
of state policy.  Nor have they sat idly by as alcoholism
has become a crisis within the State’s Native
populace.  Tribal governments have led efforts to
exercise Local Option laws to curb alcohol abuse .
Nearly one in three Alaska Natives lives in a village
or town that has restricted access to alcohol.13
This choice reflects a broader shift from federal
paternalism to tribal empowerment. 14  Prior to
statehood in 1959, the Bureau of Indian Affairs
worked with Native village councils under the Indian
Reorganization Act of 1936 to regulate alcohol in
Alaska Native communities.15  The sale of alcohol to a
Native person was a federal felony.   Id.  After
statehood, village councils lost the ability to enforce
limitations on alcohol, and alcohol -related violence
and death among Alaska Natives grew exponentially.
Id.
Local Option law s partially restore to
communities a power that statehood had taken

13 Kyle Hopkins, Wet or Dry? Shishmaref Must Make a Choice ,
Anchorage Daily News (Oct. 19, 2013), .
14 Elizabeth Hidalgo Reese, The Three Phases of the Tribal Self -
Determination Era and the Phase Out of Federal Paternalism ,
125 Colum. L. Rev. F. 205 (2025).
15 Mary T. Weiss, Wet, Dry, or Damp , The Evergreen State
College (2013), .

20

away.16  Any community, through petition and
election, can impose restrictions on alcohol that
exceed State-mandated limits.  Id.
The democratic process through which a
community becomes “dry” is deliberate, structured,
and participatory.  Alaska Stat.  §§ 04.11.491(b),
04.11.507(a)-(c).  For an established village—which is
how most rural Alaska Native communities are
classified—35 percent or more of the registered voters
residing within the village must sign a petition to
place a Local Option prohibition on the ballot.  Id.
§ 04.11.507(c).
The law also includes safeguards against
impulsive reversal: an election to remove a local
option, or to change to a less restrictive one, cannot be
held during the first 24 months after adoption or more
than once in any 36-month period.  Id. § 04.11.507(f).
These procedural requirements ensure that the choice
to go dry —or to reverse that choice —reflects the
sustained and considered will of the community.
This is not a restriction imposed on these
communities from the outside.  It is one they choose
for themselves, through a deliberate democratic
process, because they  live with the consequences of
alcohol abuse and are best positioned to judge how
serious a response those consequences require.

16 The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act created a system of
more than 200 Native village corporations, chartered under state
law.  Yellen v. Confederated Tribes of Chehalis Reservation , 594
U.S. 338, 343 (2021); see also Mitchell Forbes, Comment, Beyond
Indian Country: The Sovereign Powers of Alaska Tribes Without
Reservations, 40 Alaska L. Rev. 171 (2023).

21

Local choice is only as effective as the
enforcement tools behind it.  A community that has
gone through this process has made a considered
judgment that the threat of alcohol arriving by air is
serious enough to justify a strong deterrent, and
mandatory fo rfeiture is the mechanism the
Legislature chose to give that deterrent teeth.
These tools work.  When indigenous
communities exercise control over their own public
health decisions, outcomes have improved.17  A study
of 135 Alaska Native villages found that communities
banning the sale and importation of alcohol
experienced average decreases in accidental death
rates of 74 per 100,000 and homicide death rates of 66
per 100,000, while a control group of 61 commu nities
that did not change their alcohol status showed no
significant changes. 18  A separate study comparing
wet and dry villages from 1990 -1993 found that
Alaska Natives in wet villages had a 2.7 times greater
risk of alcohol-related injury death than those in dry

17 Ralph T. Bryan, et al., Public Health Legal Preparedness in
Indian Country , 99 Am. J. Pub. Health 607, 609 (2009)
(strengthening tribal legal foundations for public health
regulation goes “hand in hand with the tenets of tribal self -
determination”); see also Vanessa Ann Racehorse, Tribal Health
Self-Determination: The Role of Tribal Health Systems , 56
Colum. Hum. Rts. L. Rev. 183 (2025) (tribal self -governance in
health care produces better outcomes than federal
administration).
18 Matthew Berman, et al., Alcohol Control and Injury Death in
Alaska Native Communities: Wet, Damp and Dry Under Alaska’s
Local Option Law, 61 J. Stud. on Alcohol 311 (2000).

22

villages, with especially elevated risk ratios for motor
vehicle deaths, hypothermia, and homicide.19
The community of Barrow (now Utqiaġvik), an
Inupiat community of approximately 4,000 people on
the Arctic coast provides a particularly stark example.
During the four years before the community voted to
go dry in November 1994, there were 87 reported
rapes, 8 alcohol -related suicides and 45 suicide
attempts, 2,057 arrests for drunk and disorderly
conduct, 675 drunken assaults, and 229 ch ildren
arrested for drinking.  Fetal alcohol syndrome rates
were among the highest in the world.20  After the ban
took effect, alcohol -related outpatient visits dropped
by 84.7 percent.21
The inverse is equally instructive. When
Emmonak, a remote village with approximately 825
residents, loosened its restrictions and went from dry
to damp in 2016, “the community saw a spike in the
number of intoxicated people in the streets and
violence in homes.”22
Since the enactment of Local Option laws, the
overwhelming majority of subject elections—69
percent—resulted in increased restrictions, while only

19 M.G. Landen, et al., Alcohol-Related Injury Death and Alcohol
Availability in Remote Alaska, 278 JAMA 1755 (1997).
20 Kim Murphy, Cultures Clash as Alaska Town Votes on Alcohol
Ban, L.A. Times (Oct. 2, 1995), .
21 A.Y. Chiu, et al., The Effect of an Alcohol Ban on the Number
of Alcohol-Related Hospital Visits in Barrow, Alaska , 57 Int. J.
Circumpolar Health (Supp. 1) 439 (1998).
22 Alena Naiden, Utqiaġvik May Consider Allowing Alcohol Sales
on City Premises, Anchorage Daily News (Jan. 15, 2024), .

23

13 percent have removed them. 23  In other words,
Alaska N ative communities do not merely tolerate
these restrictions —they have actively advocated for
them.
“Under the terms of [the constitutional]
bargain, Indian Tribes remain independent
sovereigns with the exclusive power to manage their
internal matters. ”  Haaland v. Brackeen , 599 U.S.
255, 307 (2023) (Gorsuch, J., concurring).  The Local
Option system is a parallel expression of that promise.
Improving public safety in rural Alaska requires
“tribal, state, federal and local governments” to
“jointly identify and implement” solutions. 24  The
forfeiture statute is precisely such a joint solution —a
state law enacted with the support of tribal
communities, enforced through state mechanisms,
and designed to give effect to locally determined
alcohol restrictions.  A ruling that weakens it wou ld
not only override the Alaska Legislature’s considered
judgment.  It would undermine the sovereignty of
tribes that this Court has promised to protect.

Referendum in Northern Native Communities: The Alaska Local

International Municipal Lawyers Association and

that the judgment of the Supreme Court of Alaska
